rationale: This qualitative study codes nine Ugandan water and decentralization policy documents alongside semi-structured interviews with 93 political and technical local government officials across 22 sub-counties in three Ugandan districts. It examines two co-central legal/governance mechanisms under Uganda's 2019 National O&M Framework: (1) intergovernmental mandate allocation across district and sub-county local government tiers, centralized fiscal transfer constraints, and coordination with external actors (institutional_structure_coordination, primary); and (2) the shift from community-based management to delegated professionalized maintenance contracted out to Area Service Providers and regulated by local authorities in the absence of an independent regulator (regulatory_model_ownership). Rather than measuring household or water-point access directly, the empirical outcome analyzed is local government actors' fulfillment of assigned governance, monitoring, regulatory, and policy-compliance functions (administrative_outcome).
